key_insights: Recommends writing essays about topics you're genuinely interested in, saying it's easy in hindsight to tell which of her essays were written from real interest versus written to impress readers.
Argues different schools suit different personalities and cultures (contrasts Princeton, MIT, Cornell, Dartmouth, USC), so being authentic helps ensure fit rather than just admission.
Suggests admissions officers often have a better read than the applicant on whether they'd genuinely thrive on a given campus.
Declined to share one of her own essays (the 'community contribution' response) because it involved other people's personal information, illustrating a real ethical/privacy tension in essay topics.
Recommends starting the essay process early and warns against applying to as many schools as she did.
Says brainstorming alone took her roughly two weeks of passive thinking before she found her actual topics.
specific_numbers_or_facts: Speaker says she began writing essays about twelve months before the video's posting, roughly in early June for essays due later that admissions cycle.
notable_or_distinctive: Shows actual excerpts of successful MIT supplemental essays alongside the author's own retrospective critique of what worked and what she now sees as weaker ('cheesiest') writing.
reliability_notes: First-person anecdote from one admitted student, not an admissions professional; general advice (write authentically, start early) is broadly reasonable but not verifiable as universal admissions-office guidance, and some personal essay content was withheld for privacy reasons.
